title: What a Reporting Convention Hides: A Matched-Budget Audit of Quantum Natural Gradient with an Exactly Computed Metric
authors: Lu Wei, Yufeng Wang, Haibin Ling
abstract: Several published comparisons of variational quantum optimizers time only runs that reach a target loss, or read the verdict at a single target. Either convention could decide whether an optimizer's costlier steps pay off. We measure how much each convention changes verdicts among Adam, simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) and quantum natural gradient (QNG), on initializations held out from the selection of settings. We compute the exact metric that preconditions QNG, price every step in circuit evaluations and give every method the same budget. In a median pooled over circuit widths, cost families and a sweep of settings with common misses, SPSA needs more than twice Adam's evaluations to reach a loose target. Dropping the censored runs that miss the target hides this gap. On the global-cost family we hold fixed the settings selected for a strict target. QNG then usually reaches the loose target after Adam but the strict target first. QNG's strict-target lead disappears when the metric's simulator price, linear in the number of parameters, is replaced by an assumed hardware count quadratic in that number. We recommend charging every miss the budget and reporting verdicts across targets.
summary: This paper rigorously audits the comparison of variational quantum optimizers by demonstrating that the reported performance metrics are heavily biased by the chosen evaluation convention. By implementing a standardized cost accounting that charges every step, the authors show that the apparent superiority of one optimizer over another can vanish when reporting conventions are changed. It serves as a methodological guide for future quantum algorithm benchmarking.
main_problem: The paper addresses the bias in comparing variational quantum optimizers by analyzing how different reporting conventions (e.g., success-only runs vs. full budget accounting) affect performance metrics.
main_result: The reported performance of quantum optimizers, particularly Quantum Natural Gradient (QNG), is highly dependent on the chosen evaluation convention and target setting, suggesting that single-metric comparisons are misleading.
method: The authors conduct a rigorous comparison of optimizers (QNG, Adam, SPSA) by implementing a standardized cost accounting system that prices every step in circuit evaluations.
model_or_system: The model involves variational quantum circuits used to prepare quantum states on $n$ qubits, evaluated using global and local cost functions.
key_observables: Time-to-target ($	au$), total circuit evaluations required, ratio of medians (SPSA vs. Adam), and the number of initializations where one optimizer reaches the target first (QNG vs. Adam).
important_parameters: Circuit widths (3 to 6 qubits), target loss thresholds ($	au=0.20$ or $	au=0.01$), and fixed computational budgets ($B$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that a fair comparison requires charging every run that misses the target the full computational budget and using an exactly computed metric for QNG.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the impact of different reporting choices (success-only vs. budget-capped) on time-to-target comparisons, and tables quantify the performance differences between optimizers under various conditions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically critiques existing benchmarking practices, presents a standardized methodology involving fixed budgets and step pricing, and then compares QNG against classical optimizers across multiple cost families and target strictness levels.
why_interesting: It provides a critical methodological framework for evaluating quantum machine learning algorithms, which is crucial for researchers building practical quantum computation benchmarks.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
